questions.problem:
A  linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation. Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -7\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}56 \\ -98\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix $T$ of $T?$

| $T=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}56 \\ -98\end{aligned}] \\  & =14\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =14v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=14v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=14.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}14 & 0 \\ 0 & 14\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following represents a reflection in the line $y=-x?$
questions.worked_solution:
The correct answer is $T=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$ Indeed, consider the standard basis ${i,j}$ of the Euclidean plane ${R}^{2}$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors, as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14060608/assets/9e322e6ed1ddb8f1d094633e931cd179b7eb9d6f47acd7c7d0809f113df91b22.png)

Now, we can find the images of ${i,j}$ under $T$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{′} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j \\ {j}^{′} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=-i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following image:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14060608/assets/4a83673a409fd2e5d33b0b5f743f57af08cfb27c38e312a636179102c2172b04.png)

questions.worked_solution:

Now, we can find the images of ${i,j}$ under $T$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{′} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=j \\ {j}^{′} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Consider the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors, as depicted below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14060608/assets/9e322e6ed1ddb8f1d094633e931cd179b7eb9d6f47acd7c7d0809f113df91b22.png)

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{′} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i \\ {j}^{′} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we obtain the following image:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14060608/assets/b93bb91dae85a3e3b40a8d0ade3d4f420064aaa6926431fa7f664c977bb8fd59.png)

Therefore, the matrix represents the reflection across the $x$-axis.
